title: ISO/IEC 22123-2:2023 — Cloud Computing Concepts — Scope
text:
ISO/IEC 22123-2:2023 Scope

This document describes concepts for cloud computing. Building on the vocabulary in ISO/IEC 22123-1, it provides a conceptual framework covering cloud service categories, cloud capabilities types, cloud deployment models, cloud computing parties and roles, cross-cutting aspects, data and cloud services, virtualisation concepts, multi-CSP configurations, and the logical and physical organisation of cloud computing.

This document is intended to guide the understanding and use of cloud services by organisations acting as cloud service customers (CSCs), cloud service providers (CSPs), and cloud service partners (CSNs). It forms the conceptual basis for the Cloud Computing Reference Architecture described in ISO/IEC 22123-3.

title: Overview of cloud computing concepts
text:
Overview (Clause 4)

Cloud computing provides on-demand access to shared pools of configurable computing resources. The fundamental concepts of cloud computing centre on the five key characteristics: broad network access, measured service, on-demand self-service, rapid elasticity and resource pooling.

Cloud computing encompasses a layered set of concepts: cloud service categories describe what type of capability is offered (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, etc.); cloud capabilities types describe how the capability is experienced by the customer (infrastructure, platform, application); cloud deployment models describe the environment in which the cloud is operated (public, private, community, hybrid, multi-cloud). Parties take on cloud computing roles and engage in cloud computing activities. Cross-cutting aspects (security, governance, availability, portability, etc.) apply across all roles and service types.

title: Key characteristics of cloud computing
text:
Key characteristics of cloud computing (Clause 5.1–5.2)

Cloud computing has five essential characteristics:

1. On-demand self-service: A consumer can unilaterally provision computing capabilities as needed automatically without requiring human interaction with each service provider.

2. Broad network access: Capabilities are available over the network and accessed through standard mechanisms supporting heterogeneous client platforms (mobile phones, tablets, laptops, workstations).

3. Resource pooling: The provider's computing resources are pooled to serve multiple consumers using a multi-tenant model, with physical and virtual resources dynamically assigned and reassigned according to consumer demand. There is a sense of location independence — the customer generally has no control over the exact location of the provided resources but may be able to specify location at a higher level of abstraction (e.g. country, state, or data centre).

4. Rapid elasticity: Capabilities can be elastically provisioned and released, in some cases automatically, to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand. To the consumer, the capabilities available for provisioning often appear to be unlimited.

5. Measured service: Cloud systems automatically control and optimise resource use by leveraging a metering capability appropriate to the type of service (storage, processing, bandwidth, active user accounts). Resource usage is monitored, controlled and reported — providing transparency for both provider and consumer.

title: Cloud capabilities types
text:
Cloud capabilities types (Clause 5.3)

Cloud capabilities types classify the functionality provided by a cloud service as experienced by the cloud service customer:

- Infrastructure capabilities type: The CSC can provision and use processing, storage, networking and other fundamental computing resources, and can deploy and run arbitrary software including operating systems and applications. The CSC does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure but controls operating systems, storage, and deployed applications, and possibly limited networking components.

- Platform capabilities type: The CSC can deploy, manage and run CSC-created or acquired applications using programming languages, libraries, services and tools supported by the CSP. The CSC does not manage the underlying infrastructure but controls the deployed applications and possibly configuration settings for the application-hosting environment.

- Application capabilities type: The CSC can use the CSP's applications running on a cloud infrastructure, accessible from various client devices through a thin client interface (e.g. web browser) or a program interface. The CSC does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure, individual application capabilities, or even specific application features, with the possible exception of limited user-specific configuration settings.

Note: A cloud service category may offer more than one cloud capabilities type. Multiple cloud capabilities types enable more advanced forms of cloud services.

title: Cloud service categories
text:
Cloud service categories (Clause 5.4)

Cloud service categories group cloud services sharing common qualities. Key categories include:

5.4.1 Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): Processing, storage and other fundamental computing resources. Customer deploys and runs arbitrary software. CSP manages physical resources; customer manages OS, storage, deployed applications.

5.4.2 Platform as a Service (PaaS): Customer deploys applications using CSP-supported programming languages, libraries, services and tools. CSP manages infrastructure; customer controls deployed applications and possibly hosting environment configuration.

5.4.3 Software as a Service (SaaS): Customer uses CSP's applications accessible via browser or program interface. CSP manages everything; customer has limited configuration capability.

5.4.4 Compute as a Service (CompaaS): Computational resources for operating CSC applications, including virtual machines and containers.

5.4.5 Data Storage as a Service (DSaaS): Data storage and related capabilities — DSaaS is commonly virtualised, abstracting storage from underlying hardware to offer distribution, replication, sharding and affinity capabilities.

5.4.6 Network as a Service (NaaS): Transport connectivity and related network capabilities; virtual private networks (VPNs) providing secure networking between specific machines.

5.4.7 Communications as a Service (CaaS): Communications and collaboration capabilities.

5.4.8 Additional categories include: Database as a Service, Identity as a Service, Security as a Service, Desktop as a Service, Email as a Service, Management as a Service, Serverless Computing.

title: Cloud deployment models
text:
Cloud deployment models (Clause 5.5)

5.5.1 Public cloud: Infrastructure provisioned for open use by the general public. May be owned, managed and operated by a business, academic or government organisation. Exists on the premises of the cloud provider. Multiple unrelated cloud service customers share the same infrastructure with multi-tenancy isolation.

5.5.2 Private cloud: Infrastructure provisioned for exclusive use by a single organisation comprising one or more business units. May be owned, managed and operated by the organisation, a third party, or a combination, on or off premises. Provides the highest degree of control and security.

5.5.3 Community cloud: Infrastructure provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of organisations with shared concerns (e.g. mission, security requirements, policy and compliance). May be owned, managed and operated by one or more of the organisations or a third party.

5.5.4 Multi-cloud: A CSC uses cloud services from more than one CSP. Enables improved reliability, performance optimisation, choice of best services and cost savings. CSPs may be unaware of each other.

5.5.5 Hybrid cloud: Uses at least two different cloud deployment models (e.g. private and public cloud) that remain distinct entities but are bound together by standardised or proprietary technology enabling data and application portability. A CSC can combine on-premises private cloud and public cloud services from one or more CSPs.

title: Cloud computing parties and roles
text:
Cloud computing parties and roles (Clause 6)

6.1 Cloud computing parties: Entities that play roles in cloud computing. A party can play more than one role at any given point in time.

Major parties:
- Cloud service customer (CSC): A party in a business relationship with cloud service provider(s) for the purpose of using cloud services. May also have a business relationship with cloud service partners.
- Cloud service partner (CSN): A party engaged in support of, or auxiliary to, activities of either the CSP or CSC, or both.
- Cloud service provider (CSP): A party in a business relationship for the purpose of providing cloud services to CSCs or CSNs.

An organisation can simultaneously be a CSP and a CSC — for example, operating an internal private cloud while also using external cloud services.

6.2 Cloud computing roles: The three major roles are CSC role, CSN role and CSP role. These can be further organised into sub-roles. Roles and sub-roles are sets of activities.

6.2.2 CSC role: Includes ensuring smooth operation of cloud services, acquisition and use of cloud services, and integration with existing ICT systems. Sub-roles described in ISO/IEC 22123-3: CSC:cloud service user, CSC:cloud service administrator, CSC:cloud service business manager.

6.2.3 CSP role: Makes cloud services available. Includes providing services, deploying and monitoring services, managing business plans, providing audit data. Sub-roles: operations manager, deployment manager, service manager, business manager, customer support, inter-cloud provider, security and risk manager, network provider.

6.2.4 CSN role: Supports or is auxiliary to CSP role or CSC role or both. Activities vary by partner type and relationship. Sub-roles: cloud service developer, cloud auditor, cloud service broker.

title: Cross-cutting aspects: auditability, availability, governance, interoperability
text:
Cross-cutting aspects (Clause 7.1–7.5)

Cross-cutting aspects are behaviours or capabilities coordinated across roles and implemented consistently in a cloud computing system. They can impact multiple roles, activities and functional components.

7.2 Auditability: Capability of collecting and making available necessary evidential information related to the operation and use of a cloud service for the purpose of conducting an audit. Audit evidence includes records and logs related to the use and provision of cloud services from both CSC and CSP, maintained securely. Audits may be conducted on CSC's use of cloud services or on CSP's provision of cloud services. Cloud audits verify compliance with standards such as ISO/IEC 27001, with security and privacy certifications. Reference: ISO/IEC TR 3445.

7.3 Availability: Ability to be in a state to perform as required; depends on reliability, recoverability and maintainability. Typically a key SLO in the cloud SLA — defined as the amount or percentage of time the service is accessible and usable. Can include allowable planned downtime for maintenance. Reference: ISO/IEC 27017.

7.4 Governance: System by which provision and use of cloud services are directed and controlled by decision-makers. Internal cloud governance: design-time and run-time policies for cloud computing solutions. External cloud governance: CSA and SLA between CSC and CSP. No specific cloud governance standard exists, but ISO/IEC 38500 applies to ICT governance generally. Key governance elements: creation and maintenance of policies; effective monitoring and reporting.

7.5 Interoperability: Ability of a CSC's system to interact with a cloud service, or for one cloud service to interact with other cloud services, by exchanging information according to a prescribed method to obtain predictable results. Covers both CSC-to-cloud and cloud-to-cloud interactions. Multiple interfaces typically involved: service interface, administration interface, business interface.

title: Cross-cutting aspects: maintenance, performance, portability, PII protection
text:
Cross-cutting aspects (Clause 7.6–7.9)

7.6 Maintenance and versioning: Maintenance is the process of modifying a system to correct flaws, improve performance or adapt to a changed environment. Versioning assigns unique version identifiers to specific software states. Through DevOps and continuous delivery it is common for cloud services to be updated frequently. API changes require particular care — forward compatibility should be maintained; breaking API changes should only be introduced when absolutely necessary. Maintenance and versioning procedures are described in the CSA and cloud SLA (ISO/IEC 19086).

7.7 Performance: Non-functional aspects including: transaction rate, latency for service requests, data throughput rate, number of concurrent service requests, data storage capacity, concurrent execution threads, runtime memory available, limits on elasticity and scaling. Performance is covered by cloud SLA components per ISO/IEC 19086-1. Performance considerations are vital for reliability, scalability and optimum cost.

7.8 Portability: Cloud application portability is the ability to migrate an application from one cloud service to another or between a CSC's system and a cloud service. Cloud data portability is the ability to easily transfer data from one system to another without being required to re-enter data. Portability is rarely binary — it is subject to switching costs (see ISO/IEC 19941). Ideally CSPs adopt standard data interchange formats.

7.9 Protection of PII: Involves appropriate collection, processing and disposal of PII. A Privacy Information Management System (PIMS — ISO/IEC 27701) applies to both PII controllers and processors. In cloud computing, the CSC is typically the PII controller and the CSP is typically the PII processor. ISO/IEC 27018 establishes controls for PII protection in public cloud. ISO/IEC 19086-4 describes SLA elements specifically relating to privacy and security.

title: Cross-cutting aspects: regulatory, resiliency, reversibility, security, SLAs
text:
Cross-cutting aspects (Clause 7.10–7.14)

7.10 Regulatory: Cloud service use and provision is influenced by legal and regulatory provisions that vary by jurisdiction. Both CSCs and CSPs must be aware of applicable provisions — complicated by the cross-jurisdictional nature of cloud services. Some regulations target cloud-specific operations (logging, lawful interception, digital evidence, child protection, AI including facial recognition). The CSA and SLA are the core mechanisms for establishing regulatory compliance. Relevant standards: ISO/IEC 27050 (electronic discovery), ISO/IEC 27037 (digital evidence), ISO/IEC TR 22678 (governmental cloud policies).

7.11 Resiliency: Ability of a system to provide and maintain an acceptable level of service in the face of faults — intentional, unintentional or naturally caused. Realised through monitoring, preventive and responsive processes enabling continuous operations through failure and recovery actions (hardware, communications, software failures). Resiliency is determined by the least resilient component in the system — risk management is inherent in resiliency.

7.12 Reversibility: Process for the CSC to retrieve CSC data and application artefacts, and for the CSP to delete all CSC data and cloud service derived data after an agreed period. Steps typically involve: CSC retrieves data, informs CSP to delete copies, CSP safeguards backups until exit process completes. ISO/IEC 19941 deals with portability issues in CSC exit. Regulations in some jurisdictions place specific reversibility requirements, particularly for PII.

7.13 Security: Preservation of confidentiality, integrity and availability; also authenticity, accountability, non-repudiation, reliability. Security is a shared responsibility between CSP and CSC — the split depends on the cloud service category. ISO/IEC 27017 deals with information security for cloud services. ISO/IEC 19086-4 contains SLOs and SQOs for security in the cloud SLA. CSPs commonly hold certifications against ISO/IEC 27001 with the extended control set defined in ISO/IEC 27017.

7.14 Service levels and SLAs: The cloud SLA (ISO/IEC 19086) includes SLOs and SQOs for the covered cloud service. Details vary for different cloud service categories, cloud capabilities types, key characteristics and cross-cutting aspects. The CSA and cloud SLA define measurable properties of the cloud service; implementing a cloud SLA involves monitoring, reporting failures to meet SLOs and identifying remedies.

title: Data and cloud services
text:
Data and cloud services (Clause 8)

8.1 Data is an important element of any ICT system and this applies to cloud services. Topics covered include data processing, data flow, processing from multiple sources and data sharing.

8.2 Data processing within cloud services: The simplest form is data storage (DSaaS). Many cloud services perform analytics and other processing. ISO/IEC 19944-1 includes a data taxonomy for describing data processing within cloud services plus data processing and data use categories enabling construction of data use statements. ISO/IEC 22624 extends this framework for data-related policies and practices including data at rest, in transit and cross-border transfer.

8.3 Data flow: Data flow takes place into and out of cloud services, between cloud services, from/to devices connected to cloud services, and through edge computing tiers. ISO/IEC 19941 describes data flow in terms of interoperability and data portability. ISO/IEC 23188 describes data flow between devices and cloud services in edge computing context.

8.4 Processing of data from multiple sources: Cloud scalability simplifies bringing together multiple datasets for cross-source processing and analysis. Challenges include: data use obligations and controls; data provenance, quality and integrity; chain of custody; security and privacy; immutable proof of regulatory compliance. ISO/IEC 23186 provides a framework for trustworthy processing of data from multiple sources.

8.5 Data sharing: Increasingly organisations see value in sharing data. Data sharing is performed under a data sharing agreement (DSA) describing terms, obligations for data holder and user, provenance, quality, integrity and processing restrictions. Reference: ISO/IEC 23751.

title: Virtualisation concepts
text:
Virtualisation concepts (Clause 9)

9.1 Sharing of compute resources involves some level of virtualisation. See ISO/IEC TS 23167 for additional description.

9.2.1 System hardware virtualisation: Virtualisation of compute resources using virtual machines (VMs) involves a hypervisor that virtualises the physical resources, enabling multiple VMs to run on a physical system while appearing to have their own system hardware (processor, memory, storage, networking). Each VM can contain its own operating system, enabling different OSes on a single system.

9.2.2 Virtual machines (VMs): Isolated execution environments using virtualised physical resources. Enable multiple applications or application instances to run simultaneously on one hardware system while remaining isolated. Each VM appears to have its own system hardware.

9.2.3 Hypervisors: Software that virtualises physical resources and manages VMs. Allocates CPU, memory, disk storage and networking capabilities to each running VM.

9.3 Containers: Isolated execution environments using a virtualised OS kernel (host OS). The container software is isolated — it gets a strictly limited version of the host OS, analogous to VM virtualisation of physical resources. Each container has its own application software and runs using virtualised resources. All containers share the host OS kernel — the OS must be compatible with the host OS kernel.

9.4 Serverless computing: CSC can use cloud capabilities without provisioning, deploying or managing hardware or software resources other than providing CSC application code or data. Functions as a Service (FaaS): CSC uses execution of CSC application code as functions triggered by CSC-specified events. Serverless database: database provisioned, managed and operated by CSP with functions available via API.

9.5 Virtualised networking: Network capabilities virtualised towards applications and systems rather than underlying networking hardware. Includes VPNs providing secure networking between specific machines even on different networks.

9.6 Virtualised DSaaS: Storage capabilities abstracted from underlying hardware; can offer distribution, replication, sharding and affinity capabilities without CSC intervention.

title: Concepts of cloud computing involving multiple CSPs
text:
Concepts of cloud computing involving multiple CSPs (Clause 10)

10.1 Instead of accessing cloud services from a single CSP, a CSC can access cloud services directly from more than one CSP. Benefits include: improved reliability, performance optimisation, choice of best cloud services and cost savings.

10.2.2 Multi-cloud computing: A CSC uses public cloud services from two or more CSPs and can provide integration and management of these disparate cloud services. When cloud services from one or more CSPs are combined or integrated by the CSC, the result is often referred to as a cloud solution. Multi-cloud can be used to deliver application, platform or infrastructure capabilities types.

10.2.3 Inter-cloud computing: A CSP that uses one or more cloud services provided by other CSPs is in an inter-cloud relationship. The CSP using the cloud services is the primary CSP; the CSP whose services are being used is the secondary CSP. The purpose is to jointly provide cloud services to a CSC. The use of inter-cloud computing can be invisible to the CSC.

10.2.4 Other types: Configurations where two or more CSPs separately deliver one or more cloud services to a single CSC. Can address elasticity and scalability requirements beyond private cloud capabilities.

10.3 Considerations when using multiple CSPs:
- Identity and access management: Each CSP needs to identify users and determine authorisation.
- Policy considerations: CSPs can exist in different policy environments (jurisdictional, governance, regulatory). Resolving policy differences impacts interaction between CSPs.
- Management: Focuses on how CSC and CSPs act together — access management, billing, resource management.
- Operations: Resource allocation, broadcasting available resources and capabilities, monitoring and metering.

title: Organisation of cloud computing — logical and physical
text:
Organisation of cloud computing (Clause 11)

11.1 Logical organisation:

11.1.1 Cloud service instance: Entity providing the capabilities of a cloud service. Each cloud service instance has its own resources isolated from other instances and provides a service interface for CSC interaction. A single cloud service can create many instances (e.g. a containers cloud service creates many container instances, each with separate interaction).

11.1.2 Multiple cloud services: Common for applications to use more than one cloud service for different components. Uses include: scalability (horizontal scaling via multiple instances), fault tolerance (avoiding single points of failure), lowering latency (geographically dispersed instances close to users). Cloud native applications can use microservice architectures with multiple separate code components and data storage components.

11.2 Physical organisation:

11.2.2 Cloud service provider (physical): The CSP makes cloud services available and the CSC can create instances in multiple physical locations. Cloud service instances can exist in multiple physical locations chosen by the CSC.

11.2.3 Cloud service resources: Physical resources include computers (CPU, memory), storage components, networks and related infrastructure; organised as compute nodes and storage nodes.

11.2.4 Cloud region: Geographical area containing set of physical resources independent and isolated from other cloud regions. Aims to avoid shared failure points and provide low latency within region. Physical size not fixed — large enough to survive utility failures or environmental disasters.

11.2.5 Availability domain or zone: Logically and physically isolated location within a cloud region with independent power, cooling and network infrastructure. Minimum of three per region advisable. CSC can allocate instances across multiple availability domains for resilience.

11.2.6 Edge computing: Distributed computing with components on multiple nodes across tiers. Edge tier has distributed locations. Critical that specific cloud service instances can be placed on specific nodes for latency requirements.

11.2.7 Affinity: Placement of two or more resources close together for low latency. Resources can have low or high affinity depending on interaction frequency and requirements.

11.2.8 Geo-dispersion: Keeping resources separated to avoid single points of failure. Placing instances in multiple availability domains guards against single domain failure.

title: Cloud service categories and cloud capabilities types — mapping table
text:
Annex A (informative) — Cloud service categories (Table A.1)

Mapping of cloud service categories to cloud capabilities types (Infrastructure / Platform / Application):

- Compute as a Service: Infrastructure X, Platform X
- Communications as a Service: Platform X, Application X
- Data Storage as a Service: Infrastructure X, Platform X, Application X
- Infrastructure as a Service: Infrastructure X
- Network as a Service: Infrastructure X, Application X
- Platform as a Service: Platform X
- Software as a Service: Application X
- Database as a Service: Platform X, Application X
- Desktop as a Service: Infrastructure X, Platform X, Application X
- Email as a Service: Platform X, Application X
- Identity as a Service: Platform X, Application X
- Management as a Service: Platform X, Application X
- Security as a Service: Platform X, Application X
- Serverless Computing: Platform X

Note: A cloud service category may offer any combination of the three cloud capabilities types. The commercial cloud computing market is very dynamic and new informal cloud service categories continue to emerge.
